question: What is an array?
expectedAnswer: An array is a linear data structure that stores a collection of elements of the same data type in contiguous memory locations. It provides O(1) constant-time access to elements by index but has a fixed size in static memory.
explanation: Contiguous memory layout allows random O(1) indexed lookup.
aiSpeechText: What is an array, and what are its main advantages and limitations?

question: Difference between array and linked list.
expectedAnswer: Arrays use contiguous memory and provide O(1) indexed access, but insertion/deletion at arbitrary positions takes O(n) and sizing is fixed. Linked lists store nodes with pointers anywhere in heap memory, providing O(1) insertions/deletions once pointer is positioned, but require O(n) sequential traversal to access an element and extra memory for pointers.
explanation: Arrays = fast indexed access & contiguous memory; Linked lists = dynamic size & flexible insertions.
aiSpeechText: What are the key trade-offs between arrays and linked lists in terms of memory and performance?

question: What is a stack? Give a real-world example.
expectedAnswer: A stack is a linear data structure following the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle, where insertions and deletions happen only at the top (push and pop in O(1)). Real-world examples include browser back-button history, undo/redo in text editors, and call stack execution in compilers.
explanation: Stack operates on LIFO (Last In First Out) semantics.
aiSpeechText: What is a stack data structure, and can you provide two real-world software applications of it?

question: What is a queue?
expectedAnswer: A queue is a linear data structure following the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle. Elements are inserted at the rear (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue). Applications include CPU task scheduling, print queues, and breadth-first search traversal.
explanation: Queue operates on FIFO (First In First Out) order.
aiSpeechText: What is a queue, and where is it commonly used in software systems?

question: Difference between stack and queue.
expectedAnswer: A stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out) where insertion and deletion occur at the same end (top). A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out) where insertion occurs at the rear and deletion occurs at the front.
explanation: Stack is LIFO; Queue is FIFO.
aiSpeechText: Explain the difference between a stack and a queue in terms of data insertion and retrieval order.

question: What is a binary tree?
expectedAnswer: A binary tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure in which each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and right child. It starts with a single root node and nodes without children are leaf nodes.
explanation: Hierarchical node structure where every node has maximum 2 children.
aiSpeechText: What is a binary tree, and what are its key structural properties?

question: What is a binary search tree?
expectedAnswer: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree with an ordering property: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater. This allows O(log n) average search, insertion, and deletion.
explanation: BST enforces left < root < right ordering for efficient binary searching.
aiSpeechText: What is a binary search tree, and what is its main advantage over an unordered binary tree?

question: Difference between linear search and binary search.
expectedAnswer: Linear search inspects every element sequentially from start to end with O(n) time complexity and works on unsorted lists. Binary search works on sorted arrays by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half, achieving O(log n) time complexity.
explanation: Linear search = sequential O(n) on unsorted data; Binary search = divide & conquer O(log n) on sorted data.
aiSpeechText: What is the difference between linear search and binary search in terms of prerequisites and time complexity?

question: Explain bubble sort, selection sort, and insertion sort.
expectedAnswer: Bubble Sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order (O(n^2)). Selection Sort repeatedly finds the minimum element from the unsorted part and places it at the beginning (O(n^2), minimum swaps). Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one item at a time by inserting each element into its proper position (O(n^2) worst case, O(n) best case for nearly sorted data).
explanation: Bubble = swap adjacent; Selection = pick minimum; Insertion = place into sorted prefix.
aiSpeechText: Can you briefly explain how bubble sort, selection sort, and insertion sort work?

question: What is Big-O notation?
expectedAnswer: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation used in computer science to describe the upper bound of the execution time or space complexity of an algorithm in the worst-case scenario as the input size n grows to infinity.
explanation: Big-O measures upper bound algorithmic efficiency as input scales.
aiSpeechText: What is Big-O notation and why is it essential when evaluating algorithms?

question: What is the time complexity of binary search?
expectedAnswer: The time complexity of binary search is O(log n) in the average and worst case, because the search space is halved in each step. The best case is O(1) when the target element is at the middle of the array.
explanation: Halving the search space per iteration yields logarithmic time O(log n).
aiSpeechText: What is the time complexity of binary search in the best, average, and worst cases?

question: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
expectedAnswer: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores neighbor nodes layer by layer using a Queue and is optimal for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking using a Stack or Recursion, and is useful for cycle detection, topological sorting, and pathfinding.
explanation: BFS explores level by level (Queue); DFS explores branch depth first (Stack/Recursion).
